title: When blood groups were discovered in 1901, there was no type O: it was called C
body: In 1900 the Austrian doctor Karl Landsteiner noticed that red blood cells from one person often clumped together when mixed with serum from another. In 1901 he sorted human blood into three groups, **A, B and C**, according to which serum clumped which cells. His students found a fourth type the following year. In 1910 Ludwik Hirszfeld and Emil von Dungern renamed group C as 0, for 'null', and called the fourth type AB; that zero is where today's O comes from.

cover.alt: Black and white photo of Karl Landsteiner in a white lab coat and bow tie, seated at a laboratory bench with glass flasks

slides.prompt: Landsteiner was not sure why one person's serum clumped another person's red cells. What did he wonder?
slides.answer: Inborn differences, or damage from bacteria?
slides.detail: He wrote that it 'remains to be seen' which was true. The answer turned out to be inborn differences: the blood groups.

slides.heading: Naming the blood groups took decades
slides.note: In 1907 Reuben Ottenberg also made the first practical use of blood typing in a transfusion

slides.heading: Match Janský's 1907 groups to today's
slides.explanation: The Czech serologist Jan Janský numbered the four groups independently. In 1910 the American William Moss used a different numbering, which caused confusion.

slides.alt: A gloved hand holding a blood typing gel card with six small tubes; red cells sit at the bottom of some tubes and near the top of others
slides.caption: A modern gel card for type O positive. Clumped cells get stuck near the top of a tube; unclumped cells sink to the bottom. Here they sink in the A and B tubes.

slides.label: blood group systems recognised today
slides.text: As of June 2025. ABO, the first one found, is still the most important for transfusions.
